name: Research, Knowledge and Learning
blurb: How the field explains itself: papers and their venues, books, courses and certifications, the skills graph, the glossary and taxonomy, and the media record of talks and podcasts.

domains.name: AI Research Library
domains.blurb: The AI Research Library has two layers. The first is a curated shelf of 134 peer-reviewed and preprint papers, organised into ten topics from architectures and reasoning to bias, evaluation, security and the EU AI Act, each with its authors, venue, year and citation count, a short note on why it matters, and, where the abstract is on file, three explanations written for a beginner, a practitioner and a business reader. The second is the index behind the site's ask box: more than 1.38 million research works drawn from OpenAlex, 964,000 of them with abstracts, reaching back to 1812 and refreshed on every pipeline run, searchable in full text. Every link on a paper page goes to the paper's own home, arXiv, the journal, or the publisher, never to an aggregator. Every source cited anywhere on The World of AI is listed on the companion Sources page.

sections.name: Podcasts
sections.blurb:
This section curates podcasts covering AI research, engineering, and industry strategy, tracking each show's host, focus, and whether transcripts are published, rather than pulling from a live episode feed or download-ranking data.

Each entry is manually reviewed and its listing is checked against the show's own site, most recently on September 5, 2026, for every podcast currently listed. That means the section reflects editorial judgment about which shows are worth a reader's time, not an algorithmic popularity ranking, and it will not automatically surface new or emerging shows the way a review-count-based directory might.

As of this verification pass, six shows are listed. The Cognitive Revolution, hosted by Nathan Labenz, and the Dwarkesh Podcast, hosted by Dwarkesh Patel, are positioned as capability and strategy analysis with published transcripts. Latent Space, from swyx and Alessio Fanelli, is described as the AI engineering podcast of record, also with transcripts. Practical AI, with Chris Benson and Daniel Whitenack, and The TWIML AI Podcast, hosted by Sam Charrington, round out the applied and long-running interview side, both with transcripts or detailed show notes. The Lex Fridman Podcast is included for its long-form AI researcher interviews but only has selected transcripts published, rather than a full archive like the others. Episode cadence varies widely by show, from weekly interview formats to more sporadic long-form releases, and this section does not track episode count, release schedule, or download rankings for any of the shows it lists.

sections.name: Image and Diagram Library
sections.blurb:
This section curates freely usable images, diagrams, and interactive visualizations for explaining AI concepts, covering architecture diagrams, illustrated walkthroughs, and browser-based model explorers, rather than hosting original photography or benchmark charts produced in-house.

Each resource is manually selected and its listing checked against the source, most recently on September 5, 2026, for every item currently included. That means the library reflects a small, hand-picked set of references rather than a comprehensive or automatically updated index of every diagram available online, and licensing terms vary by source and should be checked on the original page before reuse.

As of this verification pass, five resources are listed. The Illustrated Transformer, by Jay Alammar, remains the canonical visual walkthrough of transformer architecture. ML Visuals, maintained by dair.ai on GitHub, offers an open, editable set of machine-learning figures free to use with credit. Transformer Explainer, from Georgia Tech's Polo Club, runs a live GPT-2 model in the browser with every attention head inspectable. The Distill.pub archive preserves peer-reviewed interactive explanations from the now-inactive journal under CC-BY terms. Wikimedia Commons' Machine Learning category rounds out the list with freely licensed diagrams, though licenses are set per file rather than uniformly. New entries are added by editorial nomination rather than a submission form, so a reader who knows of a resource worth including has no self-serve way to suggest it yet.

reading.body:
Of the 771 pages under this section, 553 are glossary entries alone, meaning the glossary and taxonomy is by far the largest single component of how this site explains AI to itself, more than five times the size of the 147-page research library.

The six domains here split into three functions, explaining terms through the 553-page glossary, curating external learning material through 49 pages of courses, certifications, and books, and connecting everything together through the research library's 147 papers, the knowledge graph's 3 pages, and the 1-page concept taxonomy. The video, podcast, and image library adds 18 more pages of media rather than text, a comparatively small share of the section's total.

The size imbalance between the glossary and everything else is itself informative. A reference site that defines 553 distinct terms but curates only 19 courses and 9 certifications is investing far more in breadth of vocabulary than in structured external learning paths. The data does not say how these six domains compare in traffic or usefulness to readers, only their relative size in page count.
